articles.title: South Korea's AI Chip Boom Deepens Economic Concentration Risk - briefasia.com
articles.summary: South Korea's AI Chip Boom Deepens Economic Concentration Risk  briefasia.com
articles.full_text:
Export Engine Narrows
South Korea's economy is riding an artificial intelligence wave, but the prosperity is landing in fewer hands than before. The country's semiconductor industry has captured a disproportionate share of growth as global demand for high-bandwidth memory chips accelerates, creating a structural vulnerability that policymakers have struggled to address for years.
The concentration is most visible in trade figures. Memory chips now account for an expanding portion of South Korea's total exports, with a small group of manufacturers capturing nearly all the gains. SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics dominate high-bandwidth memory production, the specialised components that power AI data centres and training systems. As hyperscalers in the United States and China race to expand computing capacity, orders have poured into these two firms at volumes that dwarf growth elsewhere in the economy.
This dynamic reverses an earlier trend. A decade ago, South Korean industrial policy emphasised diversification away from electronics hardware. Successive governments launched initiatives to build strength in biotechnology, renewable energy equipment, and electric vehicle components. Those efforts yielded modest results, but none generated export revenues on the scale that memory chips deliver today. The AI boom has effectively re-anchored the economy to semiconductor cyclicality, just as officials were attempting to reduce that exposure.
Labour Market Distortions
The chipmaker windfall is reshaping employment patterns in ways that worry labour economists. High-value manufacturing jobs are concentrating in semiconductor hubs around Icheon, Pyeongtaek, and Cheongju, where SK Hynix and Samsung operate advanced fabrication plants. Wages in these facilities have climbed faster than the national average, pulling engineering talent away from smaller manufacturers and research institutions.
Meanwhile, export-oriented industries outside semiconductors face stagnant demand. Shipbuilding orders remain below pre-pandemic levels. Petrochemical producers are losing margin to Middle Eastern competitors with cheaper feedstock. Steel mills are cutting capacity as Chinese supply floods regional markets. The result is a two-tier labour market in which semiconductor engineers command premium compensation while workers in legacy industries face wage stagnation or redundancy.
This disparity complicates monetary policy. The Bank of Korea must balance inflation pressures in semiconductor regions against deflationary trends in industrial cities dependent on older export sectors. Interest rate decisions that cool overheating in Gyeonggi Province can deepen recessions in Ulsan or Pohang.
Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
Concentration in memory chips also amplifies geopolitical risk. South Korea produces roughly 60 per cent of global DRAM and a similar share of NAND flash, the two dominant memory technologies. That market position makes the country indispensable to the AI supply chain, but it also creates a single point of failure. Any disruption to production - whether from natural disaster, equipment failure, or cross-strait military tension - would cascade through global technology markets.
Policymakers in Seoul recognise the risk but have limited tools to mitigate it. Efforts to attract foreign chipmakers have produced modest investment from Intel and TSMC, yet neither company plans to manufacture leading-edge memory in South Korea. The country's competitive advantage remains tied to the incumbents. Attempts to diversify into logic chips face entrenched competition from Taiwan and, increasingly, from subsidised fabs in the United States and Europe under industrial policy programmes that explicitly aim to reduce dependence on Asian suppliers.
Policy Inertia
The concentration challenge is not new, but the AI boom has made it more acute. Government officials have floated proposals to redirect semiconductor profits into venture funds supporting adjacent industries, or to impose investment requirements on chipmakers similar to those in battery manufacturing. None have advanced beyond discussion stages. The political economy of intervention is difficult: Samsung and SK Hynix are among the largest employers and taxpayers in the country, and their export performance underpins macroeconomic stability. Policies that constrain their operations risk immediate GDP contraction for uncertain long-term gains.
At the same time, younger firms struggle to access capital. Venture funding in South Korea remains heavily skewed toward e-commerce and consumer internet platforms, sectors with lower capital requirements and faster exit timelines. Deep-tech startups in materials science, photonics, or biotechnology face a shallow investor base and limited government procurement support. The gap between semiconductor incumbents and potential competitors is widening, not closing.
South Korea's economy is growing, but the gains are accruing in a narrower band than at any point in recent decades. The AI chip boom has delivered a revenue surge, yet it has also locked the country deeper into a dependency it spent years trying to escape. Whether that trade-off proves sustainable will depend on how long the current memory cycle lasts - and what comes after.

articles.title: Why Samsung and SK Hynix are falling even as Korea’s chip exports keep surging - Invezz
articles.summary: Why Samsung and SK Hynix are falling even as Korea’s chip exports keep surging  Invezz
articles.full_text:
powered by
Buy. Exports are at record levels, and the market is over-discounting near-term macro/foreign outflows. Bernstein still prefers Samsung among incumbents, expecting Samsung to gain HBM share, while SK Hynix faces more selective HBM progress/pricing assumptions. Samsung also has a clear catalyst: Q3 results on Oct 8 to confirm whether tight supply is flowing into earnings.
Key Risk: Samsung’s HBM transition (HBM3E→HBM4) slips and margins disappoint, so foreign investors stay sellers even after the earnings print.
Sell. The stock is being punished for HBM uncertainty: Bernstein cut its SK Hynix target on more conservative HBM progress and pricing. With foreigners already net-selling heavily (including SK Hynix and Samsung), the market is likely to keep demanding proof that HBM pricing and ramp timing beat expectations.
Key Risk: HBM pricing/ramp comes in stronger than expected and SK Hynix regains leadership, forcing the market to reverse the “HBM selectivity” discount.
- Foreigners sold 20.3 trillion won of KOSPI shares in just over one month.
- Bernstein prefers Samsung as HBM pricing and supply risks become clearer.
- Micron says over 75% of its fiscal 2027 memory output is already committed.
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell in Seoul trading on Tuesday even as South Korea’s semiconductor exports hit records, exposing a gap between the memory boom and the shares benefiting from it.
By late morning, Samsung was down 1.1%, while SK Hynix had fallen 2.8%. The weakness came despite September semiconductor exports surging 262.8% from a year earlier to a record $60.3 billion.
Fundamentals remain strong, but investors are looking ahead. Foreign selling remains heavy, US Treasury yields are above 5%, and the HBM debate is becoming more selective.
Record exports cannot overpower foreign selling forever
South Korea’s total exports jumped 83.5% year on year in September to a record $120.9 billion, with semiconductors accounting for half.
Those numbers helped Samsung and SK Hynix jump 2.79% and 3.21%, on October 1. Yet foreign investors were still net sellers.
Between September 1 and October 2, foreigners sold a net 20.305 trillion won of KOSPI shares. SK Hynix and Samsung accounted for 17.195 trillion won, or about 85% of that selling.
The pressure continued Tuesday, when foreigners had sold a net 737.21 billion won by 11:20 a.m.
NH Investment & Securities analyst Na Jung-hwan told Seoul Economic Daily that semiconductor companies’ structural growth trend remains intact, but added that “breaking through the top of the trading range will require an improvement in the macro environment.”
Strong exports provide support, but they do not automatically bring foreign buyers back.
Memory boom is no longer one simple trade
Investors are increasingly separating industry strength from company-specific positioning in high-bandwidth memory.
Bernstein expects conventional DRAM prices to rise by the mid-teens to about 20% in the third quarter, followed by another high-single-digit increase in the fourth. It also expects shortages through 2027.
That backdrop supports both companies, but Bernstein analyst Mark Li recently cut his SK Hynix target to 2.7 million won from 3.3 million won, citing more conservative assumptions around HBM progress and pricing.
“We still prefer Samsung among the incumbent suppliers,” Li wrote, according to Investing.com.
Bernstein expects Samsung to gain HBM share, while the transition from HBM3E to HBM4 may take longer than previously assumed. It also lowered its 2027 HBM pricing assumptions.
Record exports show the industry is booming. They do not determine which supplier earns the highest margins from the next generation of AI memory.
Bull case says investors may be looking too far ahead
The counterargument is that today’s shortage may prove more durable than sceptics expect.
A Macquarie sales note said memory supply could tighten significantly through 2027 and 2028, while long-term supply agreements may make earnings more predictable.
Micron reinforced that argument last week. The US memory maker said long-term customer commitments had risen to $32 billion from $22 billion in June, while more than 75% of its fiscal 2027 output was already committed.
Samsung has an immediate opportunity to test whether those conditions are translating into earnings. Its preliminary third-quarter results are due October 8.
Seoul Economic Daily said analysts expect improving memory prices and record exports to support earnings, though won strength could create pressure.
Samsung and SK Hynix are not falling because customers stopped buying memory, as Korea’s export data show the opposite.
The market is looking further ahead, weighing foreign outflows, elevated bond yields and a complicated HBM landscape against tight supply.

articles.title: South Korea rides the AI boom – unevenly - Lowy Institute
articles.summary: South Korea rides the AI boom – unevenly  Lowy Institute
articles.full_text:
A SK Hynix memory module (SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
South Korea rides the AI boom – unevenly
The economy has become more dependent on a handful of chipmakers, not less.
South Korea has been one of the clearest winners from the data centre and artificial intelligence related boom that is driving growth on both sides of the Pacific.
South Korean chaebols (conglomerates) Samsung and SK Hynix have long been the world’s leading producers of memory chips. These traditionally unglamorous semiconductors, which have become steadily commoditised, provide the storage (NAND) and working memory (DRAM) that consumer electronics need to handle data.
This all changed relatively recently, when a vital use case was found for High Bandwidth Memory (Opens in new window) (HBM), which essentially consists of multiple DRAM chips stacked vertically and interconnected. The logic chips used to train and operate large-language models require vast amounts of data to be delivered quickly, making HBM essential to their performance.
SK Hynix, which pioneered HBM, controls more than 70% (Opens in new window) of the global market for HBM alongside compatriot Samsung. The AI goldrush has diverted DRAM chips away from the consumer electronics market, leading to steady “chipflation (Opens in new window)”.
Samsung has historically accounted for around 20% (Opens in new window) of Korean exports. The AI boom has increased this economic concentration by an order of magnitude.
The greater risk may be that the focus on AI and enabling sectors diverts capital, talent and policy attention from traditional industries which are far larger employers.
In August this year, semiconductors comprised nearly 50% (Opens in new window) of Korean exports, with the value of shipments tripling (Opens in new window) to nearly US$47 billion – driven almost entirely by price increases rather than volume.
The Korean stock market index, KOSPI, whose exponential growth created a luminous backdrop for President Lee Jae Myung’s first year in office, is more reliant than ever on the fortunes of a select group of chaebols.
SK Hynix and Samsung have consistently accounted (Opens in new window) for more than 50% of the KOSPI’s value.
These developments have led to the rather surreal spectacle of Samsung and SK Hynix’s semiconductor workforce successfully securing a gargantuan US$400,000 annual bonus (Opens in new window). Less than 1% (Opens in new window) of Korea’s workforce works in the chip sector.
The size and speed of this wealth influx is unsurprisingly reshaping Korean society. It has exacerbated housing unaffordability (Opens in new window) in the Seoul megalopolis and led to a proliferation of so-called chipmaking “cram schools (Opens in new window)”.
It is also leading to resentment in a country where average wages (which are slowing outside the chip sector) still hover around US$34,000 (Opens in new window), adding another potential fissure to South Korea’s already highly polarised (Opens in new window) society.
These problems have led to introspection from some corners of the government. In May, a close adviser to Lee made an interesting, albeit rather nebulous, call for a “citizen dividend (Opens in new window)” funded by AI wealth.
In most other respects, however, Korea is redoubling its focus on AI and adjacent sectors.
President Lee Jae Myung in Seoul (Korea Net/Flickr)
In June, Lee promulgated his “Three Mega Projects for the Great Leap Forward (Opens in new window)” industrial policy agenda, which is built on semiconductors, data centres and physical AI (technologies like humanoid robots which interact with the physical world). The overarching and lofty objective is for Korea to become the world’s number three AI power.
As part of Lee’s policy announcement, SK Hynix and Samsung pledged to spend US$520 billion (Opens in new window) to build four huge chip fabrication facilities in southwestern Korea.
The 2027 budget has followed up with over US$15 billion worth (Opens in new window) of supporting initiatives, mostly focused on building the requisite power and infrastructure for these colossal fabs.
Southwestern Korea, a traditional stronghold of progressive parties, is located far away from Korea’s current chipmaking hubs, prompting allegations (Opens in new window) of pork-barrelling.
Aside from potential political motivations, a much more fundamental question is whether demand for HBM will continue to grow at such a rapid clip.
The growing calls emanating from frontier US AI labs for a deceleration in the AI development race, caused a frisson of anxiety (Opens in new window) on the KOSPI.
Another fear is that China will replicate its success in eroding Korean market share, which it has already done across (Opens in new window) major export categories including automobiles, shipbuilding, consumer electronics and petrochemicals. Surging exports of semiconductors have reversed Korea’s historic trade deficit (Opens in new window) with China.
China’s national champion for DRAM and HBM, ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) has now become China’s most valuable (Opens in new window) listed company.
Its global market share for DRAM is increasing rapidly, having reached 10% (Opens in new window), up from 4% last year. With SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron prioritising HBM development, US companies including Apple (Opens in new window) are testing CXMT’s chips for usage in iPhones – causing consternation (Opens in new window) among US senators.
Mid-September reports (Opens in new window) from the Korea Semiconductor Industry Association suggest that Korea’s lead over CXMT in HBM has narrowed from five years to three years. It remains to be seen, however, whether CXMT will be able to close this gap without access to the most advanced lithography machines, which Dutch company ASML is prohibited from shipping to China.
Korea’s instinct to protect its golden goose is eminently understandable and sensible.
The greater risk may be that the focus on AI and enabling sectors diverts capital, talent and policy attention from traditional industries which are far larger employers.
In sectors such as shipbuilding (Opens in new window) and electric vehicle batteries (Opens in new window), Korea has adroitly carved out a niche as the main global ex-China supplier despite its broader loss of market share. Even these competitive redoubts, however, are under threat (Opens in new window).

articles.title: Korea-U.S.-Japan Economic Dialogue Focuses on Security, Investments - 조선일보
articles.summary: Korea-U.S.-Japan Economic Dialogue Focuses on Security, Investments  조선일보
articles.full_text:
The Korea–U.S.–Japan Economic Dialogue (Trilateral Executive Dialogue), which brought together public and private figures from South Korea, the U.S., and Japan to discuss national security and economic issues, was held in Washington, D.C., on October 1–2, Republican Senator Bill Hagerty announced on October 5. TED, an annual event launched in 2023, involves government representatives from the three countries, a bipartisan U.S. Senate delegation, major corporate leaders, and think tank officials to discuss security and economic matters. This year marked its fourth iteration, with Hagerty—who served as a close aide to U.S. President Donald Trump and as ambassador to Japan during Trump’s first term—playing a central role.
Following previous editions in San Francisco (2023), Seoul (2024), and Tokyo (2025), this year’s meeting in Washington, D.C., was sponsored by South Korea’s Korea Zinc and Hyosung, among others. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer attended on behalf of the U.S. government. The venue was located directly across from the Treasury Department building. Amid last year’s customs negotiations, which saw South Korea and Japan commit to massive investments in the U.S., the Treasury Department stated, “Secretary Bessent emphasized how investments from the two countries support U.S. jobs, critical supply chains, and strategic industries.”
Hagerty, whose district includes Tennessee—where Korea Zinc and LG have invested—said, “Under President Trump’s trade agreements, Japan and South Korea are investing more in this region, building factories in the U.S., and creating more American jobs. As Korea, the U.S., and Japan strengthen economic and energy security, they also reinforce national security.” The business community saw participation from CEOs of major South Korean companies alongside NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang. NVIDIA stated, “CEO Huang highlighted the mutually complementary strengths the three countries possess in computing, memory, semiconductor manufacturing, and materials. These strengths, when combined, can help build next-generation artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, strengthen industries, and create new global opportunities.”

articles.title: South Korea AI Investment Plan Puts $900 Billion Behind a Survival Strategy - remio
articles.summary: South Korea AI Investment Plan Puts $900 Billion Behind a Survival Strategy  remio
articles.full_text:
South Korea has placed roughly $900 billion in planned investment behind a national push spanning memory chips, AI data centers, and industrial AI. The South Korea AI investment plan is not a single government check. It combines long-term corporate commitments with public infrastructure, permits, regional development, and research support.
President Lee Jae Myung unveiled the program on June 29 alongside Samsung Electronics Chairman Lee Jae-yong and SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won. Lee described AI and semiconductor competition as a matter of national survival, not another temporary technology cycle.
The headline figure reflects two enormous commitments. Samsung and SK Hynix plan 800 trillion won for four southwestern chip fabs. Another 550 trillion won targets 8.4 gigawatts of AI data center capacity by 2029.
That arithmetic produces 1,350 trillion won, which was worth roughly $880 billion when the plan was announced. Broader government materials place all three regional megaprojects at 1,558 trillion won after adding related manufacturing and physical AI programs.
The distinction matters. South Korea has announced an industrial map, not fully funded construction already underway. Its real test is whether companies, utilities, local governments, and workers can turn that map into operating infrastructure.
What South Korea Actually Announced
The announcement joins semiconductor supply and AI computing demand inside one coordinated industrial strategy.
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix each plan to build two semiconductor fabrication plants in South Korea’s southwest. A fab is a factory that processes silicon wafers into integrated circuits.
The four fabs form a second major production region beyond the established semiconductor belt around Seoul and Gyeonggi Province. Government officials want Gwangju and the surrounding Honam region to anchor that expansion.
Samsung and SK Hynix together committed 800 trillion won to the southwestern manufacturing base. Both companies already operate extensive production networks elsewhere, so this represents a geographic expansion rather than a replacement.
The companies dominate the global memory market, where AI servers have sharply increased demand for high-bandwidth memory. HBM stacks multiple memory dies to move data rapidly between processors and nearby storage.
That position gives South Korea leverage within an AI supply chain otherwise led by foreign chip designers and cloud companies. Nvidia designs leading AI accelerators, while American cloud providers control much of the computing market.
The country’s advantage sits closer to the factory floor. Samsung and SK Hynix manufacture the memory needed to feed processors during model training and inference.
An investment fact sheet reported that SK Hynix expects to stage spending according to demand and corporate approvals. That condition is crucial because headline commitments do not automatically become fixed annual capital budgets.
The semiconductor program extends beyond front-end wafer production. South Korea also outlined an 81 trillion won packaging hub in its central Chungcheong region.
Advanced packaging connects processors, HBM, and other components inside tightly integrated systems. It has become increasingly important as computing gains depend more on combining specialized chips.
The government also plans more than 30 trillion won in support across semiconductor research, design, testing, and manufacturing over 15 years. That layer addresses smaller suppliers and technologies beyond the four headline fabs.
Meanwhile, the data center program targets 8.4 gigawatts of capacity by 2029. The government expects investment associated with that initial buildout to reach 550 trillion won.
Projects involving SK Group, GS Group, Naver, and other companies would distribute AI computing facilities across several regions. The goal is to avoid placing every new cluster around Seoul.
Science and ICT Minister Bae Kyung-hoon said the country expects data center capacity to reach 18.4 gigawatts by 2035. The associated investment would exceed 1,000 trillion won under that longer plan.
The official megaproject overview also includes physical AI, meaning software that controls machines operating in the physical world. Examples include factory robots, autonomous vehicles, ships, and defense systems.
These elements explain why the initiative is larger than a semiconductor subsidy package. It tries to connect chip production, computing infrastructure, and industrial deployment inside the same national program.
Why the South Korea AI Investment Plan Starts With Memory
South Korea is betting that its existing memory leadership can become bargaining power across the wider AI economy.
AI systems require processors, memory, networking, electricity, cooling, software, and data. South Korea does not lead every layer, but it holds an unusually strong position in advanced memory manufacturing.
Samsung and SK Hynix together produce about two-thirds of the world’s memory chips, according to independent reporting. That scale makes their expansion relevant far beyond South Korea.
Modern AI accelerators need HBM because processors can consume data faster than conventional memory systems can supply it. Slow memory movement can leave expensive computing capacity underused.
SK Hynix gained an early advantage in supplying HBM for leading AI accelerators. Samsung has responded with new products, production investments, and efforts to qualify additional memory for major customers.
Micron remains the principal American competitor in advanced memory. Taiwan, meanwhile, holds an exceptionally strong position in contract chip manufacturing through TSMC.
South Korea’s central challenge is therefore specific. It must protect its memory advantage while gaining more influence over packaging, data center deployment, and industrial AI applications.
The new fabs are intended to preserve manufacturing scale as AI expands memory demand. The data centers create a domestic customer base for chips, networking equipment, electricity, and cloud services.
Physical AI provides another potential source of demand. Korean manufacturers already operate across vehicles, batteries, shipbuilding, consumer electronics, machinery, and defense equipment.
That industrial base creates realistic environments for deploying robots and autonomous systems. It also gives policymakers a reason to treat AI as more than a software sector.
The program’s regional design supports the same logic. Building fabs in the southwest and packaging capacity in Chungcheong spreads production beyond the existing Seoul-area corridor.
Officials also want regional data centers near available land and energy resources. Concentrating every facility near Seoul would intensify existing power, water, and permitting problems.
President Lee called semiconductors, physical AI, and AI data centers the three axes of South Korea’s next industrial era. His framing turns individual corporate projects into a coordinated national proposition.
That proposition is aimed partly at the United States, China, Japan, and Taiwan. Each has used public policy to support semiconductor production or domestic AI capacity.
The United States has funded chip manufacturing through its CHIPS programs while restricting some advanced technology exports to China. Japan has supported new plants, including investments connected to TSMC and domestic foundry ambitions.
China has continued backing semiconductor self-sufficiency and AI infrastructure despite American technology controls. Taiwan remains central to advanced logic manufacturing and the global electronics supply chain.
South Korea cannot match every rival across every technology layer. Its strategy instead begins with a position it already controls, then attempts to build adjacent capacity around it.
That is why memory comes first. The country is not trying to invent an AI role from nothing. It is trying to prevent an established manufacturing advantage from becoming a narrow supplier position.
The $900 Billion Headline Is a Commitment, Not a Government Budget
The plan’s scale is real, but the headline figure describes intended public-private investment rather than immediately available state spending.
The 800 trillion won semiconductor commitment comes mainly from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The 550 trillion won data center figure also depends heavily on private companies.
Government support covers land, permitting, power, water, research, and selected financial programs. It does not mean taxpayers have deposited 1,350 trillion won into a construction account.
That difference affects how readers should interpret the South Korea AI investment plan. It is a policy framework tied to corporate capital plans, not a completed financing event.
Large fabs take years to design, permit, equip, and qualify. Companies normally divide those projects into stages because memory demand, technology, and customer requirements can change before production begins.
A fab’s announced construction value can also include buildings, cleanrooms, tools, and later equipment phases. Spending can move as corporate boards reassess market conditions.
SK Hynix’s stated plan makes that flexibility explicit. Its southwest investment will proceed in stages based on demand and board authorization.
The same caution applies to data centers. Announced capacity does not become usable computing until developers secure land, grid connections, cooling, financing, networking, and chips.
A data center measured in gigawatts describes electrical capacity, not the number of AI accelerators installed. It also does not reveal utilization, model performance, or commercial demand.
South Korea’s government has promised faster permits and infrastructure support because those dependencies can delay even well-funded projects. Power transmission often takes longer than the computing equipment it serves.

articles.title: South Korea's Top 1% Investors Pile Into Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Exit Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix - finance.biggo.com
articles.summary: South Korea's Top 1% Investors Pile Into Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Exit Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix  finance.biggo.com
articles.full_text:
South Korea's top 1% highest-return investors over the past month aggressively bought Samsung Electro-Mechanics on the morning of the 6th, betting on semiconductor component stocks. Meanwhile, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix — whose large-scale share buyback programs are nearing their end — both ranked at the top of net selling.
According to Mirae Asset Securities' tally of trading trends among its top 1% highest-return clients, Samsung Electro-Mechanics (009150.KS) recorded the No. 1 net buy position between 9:30 a.m. and 11:00 a.m. The stock traded around ₩1.67 million (approximately $1,200), up 5.63% from the previous session. With the KOSPI hovering near the 7,000-point level in mild negative territory, it posted the highest gain among the top 10 stocks by market capitalization.
The buying momentum was driven by expectations for expanding demand for multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) used in artificial intelligence (AI) servers. Samsung Electro-Mechanics disclosed on the same day that it had signed a ₩285.6 billion (approximately $212.6 million) AI server MLCC supply contract with a major global company. Including this deal, the company has announced six long-term supply contracts this year, with cumulative value estimated at approximately ₩4 trillion (approximately $3.0 billion).
Target price upgrades from brokerages also underpinned investor sentiment. Korea Investment & Securities raised its target price for Samsung Electro-Mechanics to ₩2.4 million (approximately $1,800) on the 2nd of this month. Analyst Hwang Jun-tae wrote in a report, "We believe MLCCs, Samsung Electro-Mechanics' flagship product, have entered the early stages of a price upcycle," estimating that the silicon capacitor segment will generate ₩500 billion (approximately $372.2 million) in revenue next year and ₩1 trillion (approximately $744.4 million) by 2028.
Beyond Samsung Electro-Mechanics, semiconductor substrate and component stocks dominated the top net buy rankings among these elite investors. TLB rose 4.75% to ₩50,750 (approximately $38), ranking second in net buys, while Simmtech climbed 6.1% to ₩177,400 (approximately $130), placing third. Hana Micron also made the list at fourth, gaining 3.69% to ₩53,400 (approximately $40).
LG Electronics (066570.KS) also drew interest from these top-performing investors. As of 11:00 a.m., the stock traded at ₩231,000 (approximately $170), up 6.94% from the prior session. News that the company had signed a long-term contract to supply cooling solutions to a 5-gigawatt (GW) AI data center in North America served as a positive catalyst. LG Electronics' AI data center cooling solution orders surpassed ₩600 billion (approximately $446.7 million) in the first half of this year, and the company expects the figure to reach several trillion won by year-end.
Conversely, the stocks most heavily sold by these top investors were Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK Hynix (000660.KS). As of 11:00 a.m., the two stocks were down 0.36% and 2.39%, respectively, from the previous session. Since the two companies announced massive share buyback programs in mid-August, other corporate entities have been purchasing an average of ₩1 trillion (approximately $744.4 million) worth of shares per day, providing support to supply-demand dynamics. However, with the buyback completion window of mid-to-late October approaching, investor exodus is now materializing. At the same time, Samsung Electronics ranked first and SK Hynix fourth in foreign net selling.
On a previous-session basis, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Jeju Semiconductor, Industrial Bank of Korea, and Samsung Electronics preferred shares topped net buys, while Samsung Electronics, Doosan, Tes, SK Hynix, and TMC ranked among the top net sells.

* Editor's note: AI PRISM (Personalized Report & Insight Summarizing Media) is an artificial intelligence-based personalized news recommendation and summary service developed with support from the Korea Press Foundation. It selects and provides six tailored news items for each reader type.
[Key Issue Briefing]
■ Semiconductor ETF rebalancing to concentrate flows into chip equipment and materials suppliers: Seven semiconductor exchange-traded funds facing index reconstitution this month hold a combined 18.9436 trillion won in net assets, and rebalancing trades are expected to cluster on the 8th, an options expiration day. In the TIGER Semiconductor TOP10 fund, Samsung Electronics (005930) exceeds the 25% single-stock cap by 1.98 percentage points, forcing a reduction of roughly 209.8 billion won. Mid-cap suppliers such as Isu Petasys and Wonik IPS (240810) are expected to see buying demand equivalent to as much as 27.5% of their average daily trading value.
■ LG Electronics secures North American supply base in AI cooling market: LG Electronics (066570) signed a long-term agreement with North American infrastructure company Air Control Concepts (AIR) to supply chillers for AI data centers totaling 5 gigawatts, locking in a stable order book worth trillions of won. After cumulative orders topped 600 billion won in the first half of this year, analysts say the company could reach 1 trillion won in chiller revenue earlier than its original target of late next year.
■ AI investment scope widening to memory and power infrastructure: The chief investment officer at AllianceBernstein (AB), which manages about 1,404 trillion won, forecast that AI spending will remain substantial over the next 12 to 24 months, with the investment scope broadening into memory, power and data center efficiency. South Korean chipmakers hold a strategically important position in high-bandwidth memory and DRAM, giving them significant demand and pricing potential, according to the assessment.
[News of Interest to Stock Investors]
Key points: Seven semiconductor ETFs facing scheduled index reconstitution this month held combined assets under management of 18.9436 trillion won as of the 2nd, with TIGER Semiconductor TOP10 (10.5974 trillion won) and SOL AI Semiconductor TOP2+ (6.0157 trillion won) accounting for most of that total. In the TIGER Semiconductor TOP10 fund, Samsung Electronics exceeds the 25% per-stock cap by 1.98 percentage points, making a reduction of roughly 209.8 billion won unavoidable. Samsung Securities (016360) estimated buying demand of about 90 billion won for SK hynix (000660) and about 80 billion won for SK Square (402340), and projected inflows of around 20 billion won each for Hanmi Semiconductor (042700), Jusung Engineering (036930), Isu Petasys and Wonik IPS. With Jusung Engineering up 37.0%, Hanmi Semiconductor up 26.5% and Wonik IPS up 25.6% over the past month, some investors are wary of a pullback once the rebalancing is complete.
Key points: LG Electronics signed a long-term agreement (LTA) with North American infrastructure platform company Air Control Concepts (AIR) to supply 5 gigawatts worth of chillers for AI data centers. The industry estimates the total contract at trillions of won over three to five years, a large deal equivalent to about 5% of next year's projected global increase in data center capacity of 108 gigawatts. With cumulative orders for AI data center cooling solutions topping 600 billion won in the first half of this year, the company is now expected to reach 1 trillion won in chiller revenue sooner than its original target of late next year. LG Electronics is building a chiller plant in Windsor, Virginia, targeting start-up in the first half of next year, and is also in talks to expand its supply lineup to include coolant distribution units (CDUs), a core component of server liquid cooling.
Key points: Ray Chou, chief investment officer for thematic equities at AllianceBernstein (AB), which manages about 1,404 trillion won, forecast that AI-related spending will remain substantial over the next 12 to 24 months, with the investment scope broadening from training clusters into inference, memory, storage and power. South Korean chipmakers hold a strategically important position in high-bandwidth memory and DRAM, and supply concentration along with the necessity of accelerated computing support their demand and pricing potential, according to the assessment. Companies that resolve power bottlenecks — in grid equipment, cables, liquid cooling and on-site generation — were also cited as promising investments, while a prolonged energy supply shock was identified as a risk that would push up funding costs for the AI industry. As evidence that the current AI boom differs from the dot-com bubble, the assessment pointed to profitable companies in cloud, advertising and productivity improvement leading the actual spending.
[Reference News for Stock Investors]
Key points: According to a report by the Center for Technology and National Security (CTS), a Washington-based think tank, semiconductor plants in mainland China had secured 343 ASML immersion DUV lithography machines as of early this year, about 270 of them NXT:1980i models. China bought 89 to 90 units in each of 2024 and 2025, spending more than $13 billion, and is applying multi-patterning techniques to mass-produce Huawei Ascend AI accelerators and advanced memory. CTS warned that if the trend continues, China could produce up to 434 million AI chips a year at the level of Nvidia's H100 by 2035. The report's authors said Samsung Electronics and SK hynix could also benefit indirectly from export restrictions on China, making the question of tighter China curbs a key variable for South Korea's chip sector.
Key points: Samsung Electronics is building a semiconductor test fab on a 265,895-square-meter site in the Yen Binh industrial complex in Thai Nguyen province, Vietnam, with total investment across Samsung Vietnam Semiconductor's (SVS) first and second plants reaching 5.48 trillion won. The first-floor line of the first plant will begin equipment installation next July and start operating in the fourth quarter, while the second floor is scheduled for equipment installation in May 2028 and operation in October. Samsung Electro-Mechanics (009150) has also decided to invest 2.51 trillion won in the same complex to produce FC-BGA substrates for AI chips, giving concrete shape to a blueprint in which Samsung affiliates collectively turn Vietnam into a hub for the AI chip value chain. Under the two-track structure, high-value memory such as HBM stays concentrated in Cheonan and Onyang in South Korea while commodity memory is dispersed to Vietnam — a supply chain strategy designed to respond flexibly to shifting global tariffs.
Key points: LG and Nvidia have launched a project to commercialize a next-generation AI-defined vehicle (AI DV) platform, with cooperation accelerating after LG Group Chairman Koo Kwang-mo and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang signed a memorandum of understanding in August. Hyundai Motor (005380), Nvidia and LG have formed an "AI DV triangle" in which they handle vehicle and driving data, AI computing and autonomous driving brains, and digital in-vehicle infotainment (IVI), respectively. Hyundai Motor plans to mass-produce Nvidia-based Level 2++ vehicles from 2028, and LG Electronics IVI systems are seen as likely to be installed. LG Display (034220) is also developing automotive displays aimed at the AI DV era, including pillar-to-pillar OLED panels running from the driver's seat to the passenger seat and slidable OLED, widening the range of LG Group affiliates set to benefit.

articles.title: Pyongyang’s Ukraine Gamble: What Kim Jong Un Bought With North Korean Blood - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
articles.summary: Pyongyang’s Ukraine Gamble: What Kim Jong Un Bought With North Korean Blood  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

source_detail.name: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

articles.full_text:
Four years into Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and one of the war’s stranger subplots may be its most consequential: soldiers from an Asian country with no direct stake in the conflict, and no public declaration of belligerency, are dying by the thousands on European soil, thousands of kilometers from home.
Since October 2024, North Korea has sent an estimated 15,000 to 20,000 troops to Russia’s Kursk region, and absorbed roughly 6,000 casualties based on the intelligence estimates of South Korea and the United Kingdom. According to Ukrainian officials, North Korea may be asked to contribute tens of thousands more troops. What has Kim Jong Un bought with that blood?
North Korea’s calculus was never primarily about Ukraine, a country with which it has no border, no quarrel, and little history. It was about what Pyongyang could extract from a desperate Russia. By mid-2024, Moscow badly needed manpower and ammunition and had few partners left willing to supply either.
In June 2024, Kim and Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty in Pyongyang that included a mutual defense clause, the first of its kind for North Korea since the Cold War. Troop deployments followed within months. In return, analysts at institutions from the Council on Foreign Relations to Chatham House point to a fairly consistent list of North Korean gains: cash payments estimated in the billions of dollars, food and energy supplies for an economy that chronically struggles to feed and fuel itself, and, most significantly for Pyongyang’s long-term ambitions, technology transfers that would otherwise have been unthinkable. Russia has reportedly supplied North Korea with air defense systems, older but still capable Su-27 and MiG-29 fighters, and, more sensitively, technical assistance connected to satellite launches and naval reactor technology for submarines.
Money and hardware, however, may be less important than what North Korean soldiers are learning. South Korea’s National Intelligence Service has assessed that despite considerable losses, North Korea’s military has gained something it could not otherwise buy: live experience of drone warfare, electronic warfare, and modern combined-arms combat, together with direct exposure to Russian battlefield tactics and equipment. North Korean soldiers rotated home from the front have reportedly gone on to serve as instructors, seeding lessons from Kursk through the wider Korean People’s Army, a pattern documented in detail by 38 North. For a military that has not fought a large-scale war since 1953, that is an intelligence windfall no amount of cash could easily replicate.
There is also a domestic and dynastic logic. Framing the deployment as solidarity with Russia – Kim has publicly praised soldiers for fighting “for the fraternal Russian people” – lets Pyongyang dress a mercenary arrangement in the language of ideological alliance, useful for internal propaganda about North Korea’s rising international stature.
Before 2022, Russia and North Korea were not especially close. Moscow had, at various points, supported U.N. sanctions against Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile programs. The war has inverted that relationship entirely. North Korea has gone from a marginal, sanctioned pariah state to a battlefield-tested security partner that Russia now treats as an equal in a way China never has. The mutual defense treaty, the flow of advanced military technology, and Putin’s own visit to Pyongyang in 2024 all mark a qualitative shift from transactional arms sales to what Foreign Affairs described as a long-term strategic and ideological partnership.
That shift has complicated, rather than strengthened, the informal China-Russia-North Korea alignment that Western officials sometimes describe (misleadingly, most regional specialists argue) as a unified axis.
Beijing has watched Pyongyang’s deepening entanglement with Moscow with open unease, as detailed in a Foundation for Strategic Research assessment of the evolving triangle. China has no formal say over what Russia transfers to North Korea, and reports of sensitive technology moving from Moscow to Pyongyang without Beijing’s knowledge have reportedly fed distrust between the two communist neighbors.
Kim, for his part, has gained new leverage over Beijing: with Moscow now willing to treat him as a peer and to backfill North Korea’s economic and military needs, Kim is less dependent on Chinese patronage than at any point in decades, and better positioned to resist Chinese pressure to rein in his nuclear program, a dynamic the Council on Foreign Relations has flagged as a growing headache for Beijing.
China is wary of jeopardizing its own relationship with Europe, and visibly uncomfortable with a North Korea-Russia partnership it can neither control nor fully endorse. Still, Beijing has responded with something closer to silence than alarm, avoiding direct criticism of either Moscow or Pyongyang. The result, as Modern Diplomacy put it, is less a trilateral alliance than a triangle of powers with overlapping but not identical interests, in which Pyongyang has quietly gained room to maneuver at Beijing’s expense.
Militarily, the record of North Korean troops in Kursk is mixed. In their first months of deployment, North Korean units suffered catastrophic losses. By some estimates, 40 percent of the initial 11,000-strong contingent was killed or too badly wounded to fight within three months. U.S. officials described North Korean assaults on entrenched Ukrainian positions as “human wave tactics” that were, in Washington’s assessment, largely ineffective. Soldiers were used as bait to draw out Ukrainian drone operators, and troops sometimes took their own lives rather than risk capture, a reflection of the harsh consequences reportedly awaiting the families of anyone who surrenders.
Yet the “cannon fodder” framing, embraced early on by Ukrainian and American officials, has been challenged by military analysts who argue it understates what is actually happening. Researchers at RAND have cautioned that dismissing North Korean troops as unsophisticated fanatics risks recycling old stereotypes about Asian communist militaries. Many of the deployed units come from North Korea’s elite special operations Storm Corps – troops that, by multiple Ukrainian frontline accounts, proved highly motivated, resilient under fire, and increasingly adept at countering the first-person-view drones that have come to define this war. Ukrainian intelligence has also reported the arrival of dedicated North Korean drone units and reconnaissance specialists, a more technical role than the infantry-assault image that dominated early coverage.
Materially, the more significant North Korean contribution to Russia’s war effort may not be soldiers at all but ammunition: Ukraine’s military intelligence chief estimated that North Korean-supplied artillery shells and missiles have accounted for roughly half of what Russian forces fire at the front. Troop deployments helped Russia recover Kursk territory that Ukraine had seized in its August 2024 incursion, but North Korean units have so far been confined largely to Russian soil, with reports suggesting Moscow has been reluctant, at least officially, to send them into Ukraine proper. That distinction lets both governments continue denying direct North Korean involvement in the invasion itself, even as evidence of attacks on Ukrainian border communities accumulates.
Whether North Korean troops have changed the trajectory of the war is, in the end, a narrower question than whether the deployment has changed North Korea. On the battlefield, the contribution has been real but bounded: enough manpower and ammunition to matter at the margins in one contested region, not enough to shift the war’s fundamental stalemate. Off the battlefield, the returns for Pyongyang look considerably larger: modernized air defenses, combat-tested doctrine, hard currency, food, and fuel, and a Kremlin now invested in North Korea’s survival and expansion for reasons of its own.
Four years ago, North Korea was a country largely locked out of great power politics, dependent on China and periodically threatened with further isolation over its nuclear program. Today it has a mutual defense treaty with Russia and North Korean soldiers are gaining experience in modern warfare on European battlefields. For a regime that has always measured success in decades rather than news cycles, that may be the trade Kim intended to make all along.

articles.title: The Japanese Yen firms on a BoJ speech about AI and gives it all back - FXStreet
articles.summary: The Japanese Yen firms on a BoJ speech about AI and gives it all back  FXStreet
articles.full_text:
Bank of Japan (BoJ) Governor Ueda speaks on Tuesday at 06:35 GMT, and his first major remarks since the September 18 hike to 1.25% are the next test of October hike bets. Traders give a second hike on October 30 about a one-in-four chance. USD/JPY has crossed 158.00 in both directions in each of the last three sessions and trades just under it.
BoJ Deputy Governor Uchida said on Monday that artificial intelligence (AI) is a large positive demand shock pushing up activity and prices. USD/JPY dipped toward 157.50 around the remarks and was back above 158.00 well before the US data. He also said AI has made financial conditions more accommodative on balance, less than three weeks after the BoJ raised rates to tighten them.
A hike every three months points to December, not October
The BoJ raised its rate in June and again in September, and traders read the three-month gap as its pace. Governor Ueda said after the September hike that the BoJ's focus has moved from lifting inflation toward 2% to stopping it from overshooting. Stopping an overshoot before it happens would mean hiking in October, not waiting for December.
Wage growth is forecast to slow by a fifth in a month
Japan's August labour cash earnings are due on Tuesday at 23:30 GMT, forecast to rise 3.7% YoY after 4.7% in July. A slowdown that size would make an October hike harder to argue for. Governor Ueda speaks before the figures are out, so whatever he says about October comes without them.
The Fed's September minutes follow on Wednesday at 18:00 GMT. The Fed decides on October 28, two days before the BoJ, so the US half of the rate gap gets the first move.
The Yen's range into Governor Ueda
Resistance: The last three sessions have all peaked short of 158.50, the level the October 1 rally stopped under. 159.00, the September 24 high, is the next cap.
Support: Monday's low, just under 157.50, is the highest of the last four sessions. Friday's low, just under 157.00, marks where the payrolls dip ended.
Bias: Buyers keep the edge while 157.50 holds on a closing basis, aiming at 158.50 and then 159.00. The daily Stochastic Relative Strength Index (Stoch RSI) is near 84 and flattening above 80, so a firm-sounding Governor Ueda could pull the pair back to 157.50 without breaking the call. A daily close below 157.00 ends it.
USD/JPY daily chart
Japanese Yen FAQs
The Japanese Yen (JPY) is one of the world’s most traded currencies. Its value is broadly determined by the performance of the Japanese economy, but more specifically by the Bank of Japan’s policy, the differential between Japanese and US bond yields, or risk sentiment among traders, among other factors.
One of the Bank of Japan’s mandates is currency control, so its moves are key for the Yen. The BoJ has directly intervened in currency markets sometimes, generally to lower the value of the Yen, although it refrains from doing it often due to political concerns of its main trading partners. The BoJ ultra-loose monetary policy between 2013 and 2024 caused the Yen to depreciate against its main currency peers due to an increasing policy divergence between the Bank of Japan and other main central banks. More recently, the gradually unwinding of this ultra-loose policy has given some support to the Yen.
Over the last decade, the BoJ’s stance of sticking to ultra-loose monetary policy has led to a widening policy divergence with other central banks, particularly with the US Federal Reserve. This supported a widening of the differential between the 10-year US and Japanese bonds, which favored the US Dollar against the Japanese Yen. The BoJ decision in 2024 to gradually abandon the ultra-loose policy, coupled with interest-rate cuts in other major central banks, is narrowing this differential.
The Japanese Yen is often seen as a safe-haven investment. This means that in times of market stress, investors are more likely to put their money in the Japanese currency due to its supposed reliability and stability. Turbulent times are likely to strengthen the Yen’s value against other currencies seen as more risky to invest in.
Author
Joshua joins the FXStreet team as an Economics and Finance double major from Vancouver Island University with twelve years' experience as an independent trader focusing on technical analysis.

KLA Corporation
Dominant in patterned wafer inspection & metrology
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Semiconductor Metrology Inspection Equipment market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global semiconductor metrology and inspection equipment market is entering a phase of structural transformation, driven by the escalating complexity of advanced logic and memory nodes, the proliferation of 3D device architectures, and the rising cost of yield loss. As device dimensions shrink and new materials and integration schemes emerge, the need for precise, high-throughput measurement and defect detection has become critical for process control and profitability. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the market from 2026 to 2035, covering historical data from 2012 to 2025.
It examines demand across key end-use sectors, including integrated device manufacturers, foundries, and outsourced semiconductor assembly and test providers. The market is bifurcating into high-end, multi-modality platforms for leading-edge production and cost-optimized tools for mature nodes. Growth is underpinned by the shift from capital expenditure-driven purchases to operational expenditure models focused on yield enhancement and predictive maintenance. The competitive landscape is shaped by technological leadership in optics, e-beam, and software analytics, with companies like KLA, Applied Materials, and ASML leading.
Geographically, Asia-Pacific dominates consumption and production, while North America and Europe focus on R&D and specialty applications. The forecast horizon to 2035 anticipates a CAGR of 6.8%, with the market index reaching 193 by 2035 (2025=100). Key risks include export controls, supply chain constraints, and cyclical semiconductor demand. This study equips stakeholders with actionable insights into demand drivers, supply chain dynamics, and strategic positioning for the next decade.
The baseline scenario for the semiconductor metrology inspection equipment market from 2026 to 2035 projects robust growth, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6.8%, culminating in a market index of 193 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook is anchored in the persistent demand for process control solutions that ensure yield and reliability as semiconductor manufacturing pushes into the angstrom era. The market's expansion will be primarily driven by the ramp of 3nm and 2nm logic nodes, the adoption of gate-all-around transistors, and the increasing layer counts in 3D NAND and advanced packaging technologies like chiplets and heterogeneous integration.
These trends necessitate more frequent and more precise measurements, both in-line and at-line, to detect defects and control critical dimensions. Concurrently, the cost of yield loss at advanced nodes is escalating, prompting fabs to invest in holistic yield management systems that integrate data from multiple metrology and inspection tools. This shifts procurement from standalone equipment to integrated solutions with software and services, fostering long-term service agreements. The market will also see growth in demand from mature node fabs, particularly in automotive and industrial applications, where reliability and quality are paramount.
However, the baseline scenario assumes no severe global economic recessions or drastic trade disruptions beyond current export controls. Supply chain resilience efforts will lead to regionalized manufacturing and dual sourcing, slightly increasing costs but enhancing stability. The competitive landscape will remain concentrated among a few major players, but opportunities exist for niche innovators in computational metrology and AI-driven defect classification. Overall, the market is poised for steady expansion, with cyclical fluctuations aligned with semiconductor capital expenditure cycles.
Integrated Device Manufacturers (IDMs) represent the largest end-use sector for semiconductor metrology and inspection equipment, accounting for approximately 35% of global demand. These companies, such as Intel, Samsung, and Micron, operate their own fabs and are at the forefront of advanced node development. Currently, IDMs are ramping 3nm and 2nm logic nodes and advancing 3D NAND and DRAM technologies, which require unprecedented levels of process control. Metrology and inspection tools are essential for measuring critical dimensions, film thickness, and defectivity at each step of the manufacturing process.
As device architectures become more complex, the number of measurement points per wafer increases, driving demand for higher throughput and multi-modality tools. Through 2035, IDMs will continue to invest in metrology and inspection to improve yield and reduce costs, particularly as new materials like high-k dielectrics and 2D materials are introduced. The demand-side indicators to watch include fab construction announcements, node transition timelines, and yield learning curves. IDMs are also increasingly adopting computational metrology and AI-based defect classification to handle data volumes. The trend is toward integrated platforms that combine multiple measurement techniques, reducing footprint and cycle time.
Major companies in this sector include Intel, Samsung, Micron, SK Hynix, and Texas Instruments. Current trend: Increasing investment in leading-edge logic and memory, with a focus on yield ramp and process control..
Major trends: Ramp of gate-all-around transistors and 3D stacking in logic and memory, Adoption of computational metrology and machine learning for faster yield learning, Increasing use of in-line and at-line metrology for real-time process control, Growing focus on sustainability and energy efficiency in fab operations, and Shift towards holistic yield management systems integrating data from multiple tools.
Representative participants: Intel, Samsung, Micron, SK Hynix, and Texas Instruments.
Foundries, including pure-play giants like TSMC, GlobalFoundries, and UMC, are the second-largest end-use sector, representing about 30% of the market. Foundries manufacture chips for a diverse customer base, requiring flexible and highly accurate metrology and inspection to ensure process control across multiple product designs. The ongoing expansion of foundry capacity for 5nm, 3nm, and soon 2nm nodes is a primary driver, as these nodes demand more stringent defect and critical dimension control. Additionally, foundries are increasingly offering specialty processes for automotive, IoT, and RF applications, which have their own metrology needs.
Through 2035, foundries will continue to invest in advanced metrology and inspection to support yield ramp and maintain competitiveness. The demand-side indicators include capacity utilization rates, capital expenditure plans, and the mix of advanced versus mature nodes. Foundries are also adopting e-beam inspection for detecting buried defects and optical inspection for high-throughput surface scanning. The trend is toward integrated metrology and inspection solutions that provide actionable data for process correction. Major companies in this sector include TSMC, GlobalFoundries, UMC, SMIC, and Tower Semiconductor.
Current trend: Expanding capacity for advanced nodes and specialty processes, with metrology and inspection critical for yield and customer trust..
Major trends: Aggressive capacity expansion for 3nm and 2nm nodes, Growing demand for specialty process metrology in automotive and IoT, Adoption of e-beam inspection for buried defect detection, Integration of metrology data with fab-wide yield management systems, and Increasing use of AI for defect classification and root cause analysis.
Representative participants: TSMC, GlobalFoundries, UMC, SMIC, and Tower Semiconductor.
Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test (OSAT) providers, such as ASE Technology, Amkor Technology, and JCET, account for approximately 15% of the metrology and inspection equipment market. These companies perform back-end assembly and test services, and their role is expanding with the adoption of advanced packaging technologies like 2.5D/3D integration, fan-out wafer-level packaging, and chiplet-based designs. Metrology and inspection are critical in OSAT operations for ensuring alignment, bump integrity, and package reliability. As advanced packaging becomes more complex, the need for high-resolution inspection and precise metrology increases.
Through 2035, OSATs will invest in metrology and inspection tools to support the ramp of heterogeneous integration and to meet the quality requirements of their customers. OSATs are also adopting automated optical inspection and X-ray metrology for package-level defects. The trend is toward integrated solutions that combine metrology and inspection for faster feedback. Major companies in this sector include ASE Technology, Amkor Technology, JCET, SPIL, and Powertech Technology.

articles.title: Chip ETF Rebalancing Set to Steer Flows Into Equipment Makers - en.sedaily.com
articles.summary: Chip ETF Rebalancing Set to Steer Flows Into Equipment Makers  en.sedaily.com
articles.full_text:
Attention is turning to shifts in supply and demand for South Korean semiconductor materials, parts and equipment stocks ahead of scheduled rebalancing by chip exchange-traded funds. As the funds trim their holdings of Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) to match periodic changes in their underlying indexes, some equipment and materials names are expected to draw substantial buying demand.
Seven semiconductor ETFs facing index changes this month held a combined 18.94 trillion won ($13.3 billion) in assets under management as of the 2nd, according to the Korea Exchange on the 5th. TIGER Semiconductor TOP10 accounted for 10.6 trillion won and SOL AI Semiconductor TOP2+ for 6.02 trillion won, making up most of the total. Rebalancing trades to reflect the index changes are expected to cluster on the 8th, which falls on options expiration day.
The latest periodic change is expected to reduce the weighting of Samsung Electronics while raising that of other chip stocks. In TIGER Semiconductor TOP10, Samsung Electronics made up 26.98% as of the 2nd, exceeding the 25% per-stock cap by 1.98 percentage points. Based on current assets, a simple calculation suggests the fund would need to cut about 209.8 billion won to bring the weighting down to 25%. Samsung Electronics accounted for 24.67% of SOL AI Semiconductor TOP2+ and 24.06% of TIGER Semiconductor TOP10 Leverage, both below the cap.
SK hynix (000660.KS) sits below the per-stock cap in most major ETFs, leaving room to absorb the money freed up by the reduction in Samsung Electronics, analysts said. Samsung Securities (016360.KS) estimated buying demand of about 90 billion won for SK hynix and about 80 billion won for SK Square (402340.KS). Hanmi Semiconductor (042700.KS), Jusung Engineering (036930.KS), Isu Petasys and Wonik IPS (240810.KS) each face demand of roughly 20 billion won. Measured against average daily trading value over the past 20 sessions, that amounts to 27.5% for Isu Petasys, 14.8% for Wonik IPS, 14.7% for SK Square, 12.6% for Hanmi Semiconductor and 7.2% for Jusung Engineering. For SK hynix, the figure was just 1.6%. That means the impact on supply and demand could be most pronounced among mid-cap stocks, where the trading volume is large relative to liquidity.
Whether index constituents are swapped is another variable. The underlying indexes of the ETFs facing October changes are mostly custom benchmarks designed for specific products by providers such as FnGuide, iSelects and NICE. Unlike broad market indexes, these benchmarks sometimes do not disclose periodic changes in advance, making it difficult to identify additions and deletions beforehand. Samsung Electro-Mechanics (009150.KS) is currently absent from the FnGuide Semiconductor TOP10 Index, as is DB HiTek (000990.KS) from the FnGuide AI Semiconductor TOP2+ Index, leaving room for actual flows to differ depending on whether they are newly added.
Brokerages said rebalancing demand could provide further upside given the sharp recent gains in equipment and materials shares, though some expect a pullback once the periodic changes are completed. Over the past month, Jusung Engineering has risen 37.0%, Hanmi Semiconductor 26.5%, Wonik IPS 25.6% and Isu Petasys 9.1%. "Because the rebalancing of these ETFs overlaps with options expiration day and is therefore concentrated, investors need to watch for greater price volatility from clashing flows in the stock market," said Jun Kyun, an analyst at Samsung Securities.
